questions.prompt: The branch reaches the TCP listener, but TLS never completes. Which layer should be checked first?

choices.text: Validate the peer certificate chain and configured identity.
choices.feedback: The TLS handshake must establish peer trust before IKE can proceed.

choices.text: Inspect the remote subnet route and policy hit counter.
choices.feedback: Those checks matter after an SA exists; they cannot repair TLS trust.

choices.text: Change Phase 2 selectors to include the client LAN.
choices.feedback: Selectors are negotiated after IKE transport authentication, not before TLS.

choices.text: Increase the DPD retry count on both peers.
choices.feedback: DPD monitors an established peer and does not fix a failed TLS handshake.

questions.prompt: Both peers show an established Phase 2 SA, but branch users cannot reach the server. What is the best next check?

choices.text: Enable the TCP listener again on both VDOMs.
choices.feedback: The transport already completed and is unlikely to explain a post-SA data-path failure.

choices.text: Inspect route lookup, firewall policy, NAT and return path.
choices.feedback: An established SA proves negotiation; forwarding still depends on routing and policy.

choices.text: Replace the TLS certificate with a wildcard certificate.
choices.feedback: Certificate trust was already sufficient to establish the tunnel.

choices.text: Change the IKE proposal to a stronger cipher suite.
choices.feedback: A stronger proposal will not repair missing routes or policy matches.

questions.prompt: Auto transport never falls back after UDP is blocked. Which configuration prerequisite is missing?

choices.text: Add a second Phase 2 selector for the TCP path.
choices.feedback: Selectors describe protected subnets, not transport listener availability.

choices.text: Create a separate firewall policy for UDP 4500 here.
choices.feedback: Firewall policy does not enable the IKE TCP/TLS service.

choices.text: Enable both TCP and TLS IKE services in the relevant VDOM.
choices.feedback: Auto fallback requires the per-VDOM transport listeners to be available.

choices.text: Change the remote gateway to a dynamic DNS name.
choices.feedback: Gateway naming does not activate the fallback transport.

questions.prompt: A team expects FortiClient to use the new FortiGate TLS 1.3 VPN-over-TCP mode. What should the design review say?

choices.text: Assume any TCP-encapsulated IPsec client supports the TLS mode.
choices.feedback: Generic TCP encapsulation support does not prove support for this TLS transport.

choices.text: Replace IKEv2 with SSL VPN for every endpoint here.
choices.feedback: That changes the VPN architecture rather than validating the feature's client support.

choices.text: Disable certificate validation so all client versions can connect.
choices.feedback: Disabling validation weakens security and does not add protocol support.

choices.text: Treat this TLS mode as FortiGate-to-FortiGate unless client support is documented.
choices.feedback: The new feature's support boundary must be checked separately from RFC8229 TCP support.

questions.prompt: An ADOM 7.4 to 7.6 upgrade fails with remote certificate invalid. The stored certificate lacks PEM delimiters. What is the targeted fix?

choices.text: Reissue every device certificate from a new enterprise CA.
choices.feedback: The failure is a malformed stored wrapper, not necessarily an expired or weak certificate.

choices.text: Restore the PEM begin/end wrapper without changing certificate bytes.
choices.feedback: The parser requires standard PEM framing; the encoded certificate content must remain intact.

choices.text: Upgrade all managed FortiGates before retrying the ADOM.
choices.feedback: Device firmware may need compatibility review, but it does not repair this object.

choices.text: Delete the remote certificate and recreate all SAML users.
choices.feedback: That risks breaking dependent SAML/PKI objects and is broader than required.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates FortiManager firmware from ADOM version?

choices.text: ADOM version is the firmware version installed on the FortiManager appliance.
choices.feedback: The appliance firmware and per-ADOM schema are separate version dimensions.

choices.text: Every ADOM automatically upgrades when FortiManager firmware is upgraded here.
choices.feedback: ADOM conversion has its own compatibility and readiness workflow.

choices.text: ADOM version selects FortiOS syntax and object schema used by that domain.
choices.feedback: The ADOM schema can differ from the appliance firmware version.

choices.text: Device firmware determines the FortiManager GUI feature version in this ADOM.
choices.feedback: Device firmware constrains managed syntax but does not set the appliance GUI version.

questions.prompt: The readiness report is clean, but a device install preview later flags unsupported syntax. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The ADOM database must be corrupt because readiness passed.
choices.feedback: A clean preflight does not prove the later device-specific install is valid.

choices.text: Ignore the preview and install the package immediately.
choices.feedback: Install preview is intended to expose target-specific changes before production installation.

choices.text: Run the ADOM conversion again without changing anything.
choices.feedback: Repeating conversion does not resolve a device-specific syntax incompatibility.

choices.text: Check the target device firmware and rendered install syntax independently.
choices.feedback: Readiness is a preflight check, not a guarantee every target accepts every command.

questions.prompt: Workspace mode is enabled. What should happen before ADOM schema conversion?

choices.text: Back up the manager and lock the workspace ADOM for the change.
choices.feedback: The backup supports recovery and the lock prevents concurrent edits during conversion.

choices.text: Allow concurrent editors to finish changes during conversion in this ADOM.
choices.feedback: Concurrent writes can make the migration state inconsistent.

choices.text: Upgrade all devices and then skip readiness before conversion first.
choices.feedback: Readiness remains necessary to identify schema incompatibilities.

choices.text: Export the policy package and delete the ADOM database here.
choices.feedback: Deleting the ADOM database is not a supported readiness remediation.

questions.prompt: An indicator is Blocked in FortiAnalyzer, but the FortiGate still permits traffic. Which missing stage is most likely?

choices.text: Repeat the incident search until the indicator appears twice here.
choices.feedback: Duplicate searches do not populate the firewall's cloud feed or policy reference.

choices.text: Increase the FortiAnalyzer log retention period for this FortiGate feed.
choices.feedback: Retention does not determine whether the FortiGate consumes the indicator.

choices.text: Verify the FortiGate feed is populated and referenced by the enforcement policy.
choices.feedback: Indicator status alone does not attach the feed to a firewall policy.

choices.text: Move the indicator into a different incident severity in this ADOM.
choices.feedback: Severity does not replace feed synchronization or policy enforcement.

questions.prompt: FortiMQ connector shows healthy, but one ADOM's firewall receives no indicators. What prerequisite deserves immediate review?

choices.text: Change the FortiGate's local admin password for this FortiGate feed.
choices.feedback: Local administrator credentials are not the FortiCare account relationship.

choices.text: Create a second block_indicator playbook in every ADOM in this ADOM.
choices.feedback: A duplicate playbook does not correct account or source-ADOM scope.

choices.text: Disable all FortiGate security profiles temporarily for this FortiGate feed.
choices.feedback: Security profiles are not the connector registration prerequisite.

choices.text: Confirm the FortiGate and FortiAnalyzer share the FortiCare account and ADOM scope.
choices.feedback: Connector scope and account association determine which FortiGate can consume the feed.

questions.prompt: A block_indicator playbook completes successfully. What does that evidence establish?

choices.text: FortiAnalyzer submitted the indicator to FortiMQ, not that traffic is blocked.
choices.feedback: The playbook result proves the submission step only.

choices.text: It proves the FortiGate has retrieved the cloud feed.
choices.feedback: Feed retrieval is a separate downstream synchronization stage.

choices.text: It proves the firewall policy references the indicator here.
choices.feedback: Policy reference and traffic matching require separate verification.

choices.text: It proves the indicator has been removed from all targets.
choices.feedback: A block operation cannot prove a later unblock or cleanup.

questions.prompt: An analyst unblocks an indicator. What is the most reliable closure check?

choices.text: Confirm only that the FortiAnalyzer incident is resolved here.
choices.feedback: Incident closure does not prove feed or policy state changed.

choices.text: Confirm source status changed, feed updated and enforcement no longer matches.
choices.feedback: The end-to-end path must reflect the unblock before the incident is closed.

choices.text: Delete the external-feed object from every FortiGate in this ADOM.
choices.feedback: Deleting the object may remove unrelated indicators and is not the normal unblock path.

choices.text: Restart FortiAnalyzer to clear cached indicator state in this ADOM.
choices.feedback: A restart is not a substitute for verifying connector and feed synchronization.

questions.prompt: A port trusts both CoS and DSCP, but the DSCP map determines the queue. Is that expected?

choices.text: No; CoS always overrides DSCP on a managed port.
choices.feedback: That reverses the documented trust precedence.

choices.text: The switch randomly alternates between the two maps here.
choices.feedback: Classification follows the configured trust behavior, not random selection.

choices.text: The egress scheduler rewrites the ingress trust choice here.
choices.feedback: The scheduler services queues after classification; it does not choose the trust source.

choices.text: Yes; DSCP trust takes precedence when both trust sources are enabled.
choices.feedback: The FortiSwitch QoS trust behavior gives DSCP precedence over CoS.

questions.prompt: Where should ordinary EF voice traffic be mapped when queue 7 is reserved?

choices.text: Use dedicated data queue such as queue 5 and preserve queue 7.
choices.feedback: Queue 7 is reserved for switch control and critical management traffic.

choices.text: Map EF into queue 7 because it is the highest number.
choices.feedback: Queue 7 protection is more important than using the highest queue number for user data.

choices.text: Map EF to queue 0 and rely on the next hop.
choices.feedback: Queue 0 is the lowest queue and does not express the intended priority.

choices.text: Disable the switch control queue to free bandwidth on this port.
choices.feedback: Disabling control protection can destabilize FortiLink and control protocols.

questions.prompt: Lower-priority queues starve whenever voice traffic is busy under strict scheduling. Which adjustment addresses the scheduler behavior?

choices.text: Increase the voice DSCP marking from EF to CS7.
choices.feedback: Changing the mark does not remove strict-priority starvation.

choices.text: Use weighted scheduling with deliberate weights for the required classes.
choices.feedback: WRR allocates service across queues rather than always exhausting lower queues.

choices.text: Move all user traffic into queue 7 here.
choices.feedback: Queue 7 is reserved and should not carry ordinary data.

choices.text: Increase the tail-drop threshold on every queue here.
choices.feedback: Queue depth does not change strict scheduling's service order.

questions.prompt: A model accepts a QoS policy but ignores configured WRED or minimum-rate settings. What should be checked?

choices.text: The FortiGate's WAN Performance SLA settings on this port.
choices.feedback: WAN SLA probes do not determine switch egress queue capabilities.

choices.text: The user's DSCP marking on the workstation only.
choices.feedback: Marking cannot enable a hardware feature the model does not support.

choices.text: The model's feature matrix and ASIC-specific QoS capabilities.
choices.feedback: QoS parameters vary by switch model and hardware implementation.

choices.text: The RADIUS shared secret on the switch here.
choices.feedback: RADIUS authentication is unrelated to egress scheduler feature support.

questions.prompt: A radio sniffer PCAP contains no frames from the affected client. What should be checked before declaring the client silent?

choices.text: Verify the radio channel, width and MAC/frame filters match the client.
choices.feedback: The capture sees only frames on the configured channel and allowed filters.

choices.text: Restart FortiAnalyzer to rebuild the wireless event database here.
choices.feedback: FortiAnalyzer log indexing does not change what the radio captured.

choices.text: Change the AP's CAPWAP control port to UDP 5247.
choices.feedback: CAPWAP transport ports do not correct an over-the-air channel/filter mismatch.

choices.text: Increase the FortiGate firewall session TTL for this capture.
choices.feedback: Session timeout does not determine radio packet-sniffer visibility.

questions.prompt: The AP joins the controller, but the problem is CAPWAP DTLS disconnects. Which capture point is appropriate?

choices.text: Place the 5 GHz radio into sniffer mode on the client channel.
choices.feedback: That captures 802.11 air frames, not the AP-controller transport.

choices.text: Capture only DHCP traffic from the wireless client on this radio.
choices.feedback: DHCP may show addressing but not the CAPWAP DTLS exchange.

choices.text: Capture the wired AP-to-controller CAPWAP control and data path here.
choices.feedback: A wired capture can show the DTLS/CAPWAP transport that an over-air sniffer cannot.

choices.text: Inspect the AP's beacon interval and probe response rate here.
choices.feedback: Those radio parameters do not explain a controller tunnel disconnect.

questions.prompt: An operator needs to change the radio profile after capturing. What must happen first?

choices.text: Leave the capture running while applying the new profile.
choices.feedback: Changing radio mode can terminate the capture before it is saved.

choices.text: Stop the capture and save the streamed PCAP locally.
choices.feedback: The browser-streamed capture is not stored persistently on FortiGate.

choices.text: Export the FortiGate configuration instead of the packet capture.
choices.feedback: A configuration backup does not contain the streamed over-air frames.

choices.text: Restart the AP and expect the browser to retain the file.
choices.feedback: The browser stream is not a persistent FortiGate PCAP repository.

questions.prompt: A single AP must capture 2.4 GHz and 6 GHz simultaneously. What design is supported?

choices.text: Use one radio with two channel widths configured together on this radio.
choices.feedback: A radio listens on one selected channel/width during a capture.

choices.text: Start two simultaneous captures from the same AP profile on this radio.
choices.feedback: The AP supports only one capture session at a time.

choices.text: Mirror the FortiGate LAN port into the AP radio on this radio.
choices.feedback: A wired mirror cannot make one radio receive two RF channels.

choices.text: Use separate AP radios/devices because one radio per AP can sniff at time.
choices.feedback: The capture consumes a radio and cannot monitor two channels simultaneously.

questions.prompt: An enrolled Intune laptop reaches the captive portal but remains an unknown host. Which setting is the first check?

choices.text: Enable application inventory updates so unknown hosts become registered.
choices.feedback: Application inventory is retrieved for hosts already present in the FortiNAC database.

choices.text: Enable health revalidation on connect before creating the host record.
choices.feedback: Health revalidation refreshes posture for a known host; it is not the registration trigger.

choices.text: Enable on-demand registration so FortiNAC queries MDM for unknown hosts.
choices.feedback: On-demand registration performs the MDM lookup when an unknown host reaches the captive portal.

choices.text: Move the connector to each server and disable scheduled polling.
choices.feedback: Connector placement changes data distribution, not the on-demand registration control.

questions.prompt: Every FortiNAC server managed by a Manager needs the same MDM host records. Where should the connector run?

choices.text: Configure each managed server separately to avoid Manager fan-out.
choices.feedback: That causes each server to poll the MDM service independently and increases upstream API requests.

choices.text: Configure the connector on FortiNAC Manager for shared host records.
choices.feedback: The Manager polls once and copies MDM host records to its managed FortiNAC servers after each poll.

choices.text: Enable Remove Hosts so records replicate across managed servers.
choices.feedback: Remove Hosts is deletion reconciliation, not a host-record distribution mechanism.

choices.text: Enable proxy communication because Manager polling requires an HTTP proxy.
choices.feedback: The FortiNAC MDM Services guide explicitly states that proxy communication is not supported.

questions.prompt: Last Poll advances after each attempt, but Last Successful Poll remains old. What does that indicate?

choices.text: The connector cannot resolve its configured MDM vendor hostname.
choices.feedback: DNS failure is one possible cause, but the timestamp difference alone does not isolate name resolution.

choices.text: The poll succeeds, but host policy matching is failing.
choices.feedback: A successful poll should advance Last Successful Poll even if a later NAC policy fails.

choices.text: The host record is absent because on-demand registration is disabled.
choices.feedback: On-demand registration affects unknown-host lookup, not the success timestamp of scheduled polling.

choices.text: The last poll ran, but the last successful poll is stale.
choices.feedback: The connector is attempting polls but has not retrieved data successfully since the older successful timestamp.

questions.prompt: Health-status queries are overwhelming the MDM API at busy login periods. Which adjustment best reduces load?

choices.text: Use daily automatic registration polling to retrieve health status less often.
choices.feedback: The guide recommends less frequent automatic registration polling instead of querying MDM on every connection.

choices.text: Enable health revalidation on every connection to reduce API requests.
choices.feedback: Per-connect revalidation increases API requests and may exceed the MDM platform's capacity.

choices.text: Disable polling and rely on the last successful inventory snapshot.
choices.feedback: Disabling polling leaves host inventory and health data stale rather than controlling query frequency.

choices.text: Increase application inventory frequency to refresh compliance more quickly.
choices.feedback: Application inventory adds more API work and does not replace health-status polling.

questions.prompt: FortiNAC-F records Vulnerability Scan Incomplete after polling a configured scan. What is the likely boundary?

choices.text: The scanner API credentials were rejected during initial connection setup.
choices.feedback: Credential rejection is a connector connection failure, not an incomplete scan result.

choices.text: The scanner poll found no result because the vendor scan was not run.
choices.feedback: The event means FortiNAC-F requested results but the vendor had no result because the scan was not executed.

choices.text: The host was deliberately placed in the Vulnerability Exceptions Group.
choices.feedback: An exception group produces an ignored/override path, not an absent vendor scan result.

choices.text: The scan passed because its configured failure threshold was too high.
choices.feedback: A threshold is evaluated after a result is retrieved; it cannot create a missing scan result.

questions.prompt: Qualys refuses a targeted rescan although the FortiNAC-F connector test succeeds. What should be checked?

choices.text: Increase the FortiNAC-F polling interval to avoid API throttling.
choices.feedback: A successful connector test and a request-refused event point first to target eligibility, not polling frequency.

choices.text: Change the scanner account password and repeat the test.
choices.feedback: The connection test already succeeded, so credentials are not the strongest explanation.

choices.text: Add a second scan with the same target IP range.
choices.feedback: A duplicate scan does not register the target in the Qualys asset inventory.

choices.text: Add the target IP to Qualys Asset Address Management.
choices.feedback: Qualys requires the target IP to be in Asset Address Management before the configured rescan can complete.

questions.prompt: A retrieved scan exceeds its severity threshold. Which mapping produces the intended NAC posture?

choices.text: Map Vulnerability Scan Failed to At Risk and Passed to Safe.
choices.feedback: The documented workflow maps the failed event to At Risk and the passed event to Safe through an Admin Scan.

choices.text: Map Vulnerability Scan Incomplete to Safe and remove the scanner.
choices.feedback: Incomplete means no vendor result was available; it does not establish a clean scan.

choices.text: Use the connector Test button as the enforcement action.
choices.feedback: Test Connection validates the API path and does not change host security state.

choices.text: Add every failed host to the Vulnerability Exceptions Group.
choices.feedback: The exception group deliberately bypasses normal scan-based access enforcement.

questions.prompt: A host in the Vulnerability Exceptions Group shows Passed despite a failed vendor scan. How should this be interpreted?

choices.text: Exceptions suppress only notification while failed hosts remain isolated.
choices.feedback: The documented exception group allows hosts onto the network regardless of scan result.

choices.text: Exceptions delete the scan results stored by the vendor platform.
choices.feedback: The exception group changes FortiNAC-F's handling, not the scanner's stored findings.

choices.text: Exception-group hosts remain allowed and can display Passed in Host View.
choices.feedback: The Host View Passed state is an exception override, not proof of a clean vendor scan.

choices.text: Exceptions raise the configured failure threshold for every other host.
choices.feedback: The exception group is a host-level bypass and does not change other scan thresholds.

questions.prompt: An automation job must create a cohort of local users through the FortiAuthenticator 8.0 API. Which endpoint method is supported?

choices.text: Use CSV import because it supports the same batch endpoint.
choices.feedback: CSV import/export is a separate resource and has different behavior from the Local Users REST collection.

choices.text: Create one local-user request for every account individually.
choices.feedback: The 8.0 enhancement adds a collection-level method for creating multiple local users.

choices.text: Use PATCH on the usergroups collection to create accounts.
choices.feedback: User Groups is a different resource and PATCH does not create local-user records.

choices.text: POST the batch to the localusers collection endpoint.
choices.feedback: FortiAuthenticator 8.0 adds collection-level POST on /api/v1/localusers/ for multiple local users.

questions.prompt: What does the X-Request-ID header provide for a FortiAuthenticator REST operation?

choices.text: It accepts arbitrary Unicode and can exceed 128 characters.
choices.feedback: The guide restricts it to ASCII letters, digits, hyphen, and underscore, with a 64-character maximum.

choices.text: It accepts limited ASCII characters and is echoed in response metadata.
choices.feedback: The response example returns the supplied value in meta.request_id for request correlation.

choices.text: It encrypts the request body and replaces API authentication.
choices.feedback: The header is a correlation value; HTTPS and API-admin authentication remain separate controls.

choices.text: It is required only for GET requests on local users.
choices.feedback: It is optional and supported for GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE on listed resources.

questions.prompt: A recent CSV import cleared certificate binding on existing users. What should an engineer infer about REST batch operations?

choices.text: The REST endpoint always clears RADIUS attributes during POST.
choices.feedback: The Community case concerns CSV import and does not establish identical behavior for REST batch requests.

choices.text: The CSV issue proves bulk REST operations cannot preserve certificates.
choices.feedback: The CSV import path is separate from the collection-level REST API methods.

choices.text: The CSV path is separate; verify certificate binding after bulk changes.
choices.feedback: The scenario is a useful post-change control, but it must not be generalized to a different API resource.

choices.text: Disable all RADIUS attributes before importing any user records.
choices.feedback: Removing authorization data is not a safe workaround for an import-preservation issue.

questions.prompt: A bulk DELETE job timed out and the automation cannot tell which accounts were removed. What is safest?

choices.text: Use DELETE on the localusers collection after verifying the staged target set.
choices.feedback: Read the target cohort first, retain the request ID, then reconcile actual state before retrying an ambiguous delete.

choices.text: Use PATCH on the localusers collection to remove selected accounts.
choices.feedback: The documented bulk delete method is DELETE on the Local Users collection.

choices.text: Delete the whole user database and recreate the API administrator.
choices.feedback: That is destructive and unrelated to reconciling one ambiguous batch operation.

choices.text: Use POST with an empty body to remove selected local users.
choices.feedback: POST creates users; it is not the documented collection-level delete method.

questions.prompt: A secret is checked out, but the user still lacks local administrator rights. What evidence should be checked first?

choices.text: Review the script result, WinRM reachability and target group membership.
choices.feedback: Checkout can continue with a warning even when the elevation script fails.

choices.text: Increase the secret's concurrent launch limit on the target.
choices.feedback: Launch concurrency does not prove the remote PowerShell script succeeded.

choices.text: Change the RDP target from FQDN to IP only.
choices.feedback: Target naming does not repair WinRM or group modification rights.

choices.text: Disable check-in scripts until the user is elevated.
choices.feedback: Disabling de-elevation increases risk and does not fix checkout execution.

questions.prompt: The check-in script removed group membership, but the open RDP session still has elevated rights. Why?

choices.text: FortiPAM must restart the appliance to clear cached group membership here.
choices.feedback: The token belongs to the Windows session, not the FortiPAM appliance.

choices.text: The user should check out the secret again immediately on the target.
choices.feedback: Another checkout would reapply privilege rather than refresh the token.

choices.text: The target must be removed from Active Directory for this secret.
choices.feedback: The group membership is already removed; the session token is stale.

choices.text: existing Windows logon token must be refreshed by signing out and back in.
choices.feedback: Windows group membership changes are reflected in a new logon token.

questions.prompt: FortiPAM reports a checkout-script warning but allows the secret checkout. What should the operator conclude?

choices.text: The user definitely received administrator rights because checkout succeeded.
choices.feedback: Checkout state and script success are separate results.

choices.text: The Windows target is offline because every warning means WinRM failed.
choices.feedback: The warning can have script, credential or WinRM causes; confirm evidence.

choices.text: The secret workflow continued; target-side privilege elevation still needs verification.
choices.feedback: FortiPAM documents that script failure does not block checkout/check-in.

choices.text: The check-in script will automatically repair the checkout script.
choices.feedback: Check-in runs a separate removal script and does not prove elevation occurred.

questions.prompt: Which account does FortiPAM try first when executing a JIT PowerShell script?

choices.text: The logged-in user's standard RDP account in every case.
choices.feedback: The script needs an account with rights to modify the target group.

choices.text: A privileged account defined on the target in the secret.
choices.feedback: That is the documented first choice before the associated secret account.

choices.text: The FortiPAM local administrator account on the appliance.
choices.feedback: The script executes remotely on the target using resolved target credentials.

choices.text: A domain controller's krbtgt account for this secret.
choices.feedback: The feature does not use the domain ticket-granting account as its script credential.

questions.prompt: A Supervisor's CMDB is stale, but PostgreSQL and FortiSIEM processes are running. What should be inspected?

choices.text: Only the FortiSIEM EventDB disk utilization on this node.
choices.feedback: EventDB storage is separate from the PostgreSQL CMDB replication path.

choices.text: Patroni timeline, replica streaming state and PostgreSQL replication views.
choices.feedback: A running replica can still be on an old timeline and no longer stream WAL.

choices.text: Only the Supervisor GUI health widget on this node.
choices.feedback: The community case shows the widget can report Normal while CMDB is stale.

choices.text: Only the number of active collectors on this node.
choices.feedback: Collector connectivity does not prove CMDB WAL replication.

questions.prompt: Which node is safe to reinitialize when one replica diverges after failover?

choices.text: Only the affected replica, using a confirmed healthy current leader as source.
choices.feedback: Reinit rebuilds the replica and must never target the leader.

choices.text: Reinitialize the current DB leader so it adopts the replica timeline.
choices.feedback: The leader is authoritative; rebuilding it risks the healthy database copy.

choices.text: Reinitialize every Supervisor to align all timelines for the current timeline.
choices.feedback: A cluster-wide reinit is destructive and unnecessary for one divergent replica.

choices.text: Reinitialize the node with the lowest hostname for the current timeline.
choices.feedback: Hostname order has no relationship to the authoritative replication source.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates CMDB and EventDB replication in the EventDB HA architecture?

choices.text: Both CMDB and EventDB are replicated only by etcd.
choices.feedback: etcd elects leaders; it is not the data replication engine for both stores.

choices.text: EventDB rsync repairs a stale PostgreSQL CMDB replica.
choices.feedback: Rsync of event files does not repair PostgreSQL WAL streaming.

choices.text: The Replication Leader is always the PostgreSQL DB Leader.
choices.feedback: The file replication leader and database leader are separate roles.

choices.text: PostgreSQL CMDB uses Patroni; local EventDB data uses rsync replication.
choices.feedback: The architecture describes separate mechanisms for database and event files.

questions.prompt: `pg_stat_replication` on the leader shows no streaming row for a replica. What does that establish?

choices.text: That the replica's FortiSIEM service process is stopped here.
choices.feedback: PostgreSQL can be running while its replication connection is absent.

choices.text: That the EventDB disk is full for the current timeline.
choices.feedback: EventDB capacity is a different subsystem from PostgreSQL replication.

choices.text: That replica is not currently streaming WAL from the queried leader.
choices.feedback: The absence of a streaming row is direct replication-state evidence.

choices.text: That the CMDB has already converged for the current timeline.
choices.feedback: No streaming row is evidence against convergence, not proof of it.

questions.prompt: A user in the Philippines connects to Jakarta despite a Singapore-first regional rule. What is the strongest first hypothesis?

choices.text: The FortiClient endpoint's private RFC1918 address is mapped to Jakarta.
choices.feedback: Regional selection uses public location context, not the endpoint's private LAN address.

choices.text: The Singapore PoP is always disabled when Tokyo is configured.
choices.feedback: The priority list does not automatically disable the first entry.

choices.text: recursive DNS resolver is geolocated in Indonesia and influences location decision.
choices.feedback: The turbo FQDN may resolve according to resolver egress and EDNS context.

choices.text: The firewall policy at the user's home router rewrites the country field.
choices.feedback: The Community scenario points to resolver location, not a home firewall country field.

questions.prompt: How long can on-prem regional-compliance failover typically take after gateway failure?

choices.text: Approximately three to eight minutes, including detection and DNS cache expiry.
choices.feedback: Health checks take one to three minutes and the DNS TTL is 300 seconds.

choices.text: It is immediate because FortiSASE uses BGP route withdrawal.
choices.feedback: The documented failover uses ICMP health checks and DNS record updates.

choices.text: It waits for the next daily MDM polling interval.
choices.feedback: MDM polling is unrelated to regional tunnel health checks.

choices.text: It takes exactly thirty seconds after the first failed ping.
choices.feedback: The documented timing includes detection and the 300-second DNS TTL.

questions.prompt: A country matches a Regional compliance rule, but the primary tunnel fails. Where should the backup PoP be configured?

choices.text: Rely on automatic fallback to the geographically closest PoP.
choices.feedback: Automatic closest-PoP fallback applies when no regional rule is selected.

choices.text: Add the backup PoP explicitly to that rule's permitted-connection priority list.
choices.feedback: A matched rule tries only the connections explicitly listed in its priority table.

choices.text: Change the endpoint's SSO identity provider before tunnel selection.
choices.feedback: SSO identity does not add an alternate tunnel target.

choices.text: Disable Regional access to FortiSASE for all countries here.
choices.feedback: That removes the geofence gate rather than adding a permitted fallback.

questions.prompt: Which gate runs before FortiSASE selects a Regional compliance rule?

choices.text: Permitted connection priority is evaluated before source country.
choices.feedback: Priority is applied only after a matching rule is selected.

choices.text: On-prem gateway ICMP health check chooses the user's country.
choices.feedback: Health checks assess gateway availability, not source-country eligibility.

choices.text: FortiClient SAML group membership determines the geofence rule.
choices.feedback: The rule selection is based on regional source matching, not SAML group membership.

choices.text: Regional access to FortiSASE allow/deny evaluation for this region.
choices.feedback: The source region must first be allowed to connect to FortiSASE.

questions.prompt: After upgrading to FortiOS 8.0, old speed-test retry/retry-pause commands are absent. What is expected?

choices.text: The schedule must be recreated as a Performance SLA probe.
choices.feedback: Speed-test scheduling and Performance SLA are separate mechanisms.

choices.text: The interface shaper now controls every speed-test packet for this interface.
choices.feedback: Speed-test traffic bypasses ordinary interface shaping for measurement.

choices.text: The speed test is disabled permanently after upgrade for this interface.
choices.feedback: The feature remains available with the updated configuration model.

choices.text: FortiGate and backend coordinate retry timing; the old explicit knobs were removed.
choices.feedback: The 8.0 feature moves retry coordination into the backend interaction.

questions.prompt: A speed-test packet capture shows throughput beyond the interface shaper's configured rate. Is that necessarily a fault?

choices.text: Yes; every packet must be subject to the same application shaper.
choices.feedback: The documented speed-test path is treated separately from ordinary application traffic.

choices.text: The DSCP marking must be wrong after the scheduled test.
choices.feedback: DSCP marking does not explain the test's shaping bypass behavior.

choices.text: No; speed-test traffic bypasses the ordinary interface traffic shaper.
choices.feedback: The test is intended to measure the path rather than be throttled by the shaper.

choices.text: The WAN member must be removed from SD-WAN here.
choices.feedback: A measurement packet exceeding the application shaper does not prove member failure.

questions.prompt: A speed-test result is consistently equal to the configured minimum. What should be compared?

choices.text: Raw measurement versus update-inbandwidth/outbandwidth minimum and maximum bounds.
choices.feedback: The applied value may be clamped by the configured interface bounds.

choices.text: Only the SLA latency threshold after the scheduled test.
choices.feedback: Latency threshold does not explain bandwidth result clamping.

choices.text: Only the FortiGate license expiration date for this interface.
choices.feedback: Licensing is not the first explanation for a configured result floor.

choices.text: Only the peer's BGP local preference for this interface.
choices.feedback: BGP preference chooses paths; it does not clamp the reported bandwidth value.

questions.prompt: The scheduled test succeeds, but business applications still have high loss and latency. What should be examined separately?

choices.text: Repeat the speed test every minute until the issue disappears.
choices.feedback: More measurements do not replace SLA and policy-path diagnosis.

choices.text: Performance SLA state, SD-WAN rule selection and ordinary traffic shaping.
choices.feedback: A bandwidth test does not prove latency/loss health or application steering.

choices.text: Increase the speed-test minimum to match the circuit contract.
choices.feedback: A higher floor can hide low measured throughput rather than repair it.

choices.text: Disable all SD-WAN rules and use static routes.
choices.feedback: That removes the steering logic without identifying the failing service.

questions.prompt: FortiMQ connector is Active, but a FortiGate feed remains empty. Which sequence best isolates the gap?

choices.text: Check same FortiCare account, source ADOM, cloud-feed sync and feed update time.
choices.feedback: These are separate prerequisites between connector health and firewall retrieval.

choices.text: Rebuild the FortiGate firewall policy before checking the feed here.
choices.feedback: A policy cannot match an indicator that has not arrived in the feed.

choices.text: Delete the FortiAnalyzer ADOM and recreate all devices for this path.
choices.feedback: That is a destructive response to an unverified scope or sync issue.

choices.text: Change the indicator from IP to MAC without checking its type.
choices.feedback: Changing type can make the indicator less relevant to the traffic path.

questions.prompt: A user batch is correlated in FAC, but the endpoint remains unknown in NAC. Which evidence pair best separates the two systems?

choices.text: FAC request ID proves authentication; NAC poll proves policy enforcement.
choices.feedback: The request ID is not authentication evidence, and an MDM poll does not prove a policy was enforced.

choices.text: FAC request ID correlates user changes; NAC poll timestamps prove MDM retrieval.
choices.feedback: The FAC request ID traces the API operation, while Last Successful Poll records successful MDM data retrieval; host registration and policy still need separate checks.

choices.text: Both systems use the same API endpoint and shared credentials.
choices.feedback: FortiAuthenticator Local Users and FortiNAC MDM connectors are separate services with separate credentials and APIs.

choices.text: A successful FAC POST guarantees the NAC host is compliant.
choices.feedback: A local FAC user record does not create an MDM host record or establish endpoint compliance.
